Theoretical background of the mhn package

Source: vignettes/theory.Rmd
theory.Rmd

Scope

This vignette is the theoretical companion to Introduction to the mhn Package. The Introduction shows what the four exported functions (dmhn / pmhn / qmhn / rmhn) and their moment helpers do; this note develops the mathematical and algorithmic theory the package implements. We summarise the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) family, the Fox–Wright \(\Psi\) function that appears in its normalising constant, and the two sampling schemes the package draws on — Sun, Kong & Pal (2023) and Gao & Wang (2025).

We deliberately keep the treatment compact. Full proofs and the finer numerical considerations live in the original papers (see References). Two implementation-relevant points — the typesetting errata in Sun et al. (2023) and how the package handles them, and the benchmark-driven rationale for the rmhn(method = "auto") crossovers — are inserted in §4 and §7 where they are most relevant.

The MHN(\(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\)) family

The MHN distribution has support \((0, \infty)\) and density

\[f(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \frac{2 \beta^{\alpha/2} \, x^{\alpha-1} \, \exp(-\beta x^2 + \gamma x)} {\Psi[\alpha/2,\, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]}, \qquad x > 0,\]

with \(\alpha > 0\), \(\beta > 0\), \(\gamma \in \mathbb{R}\). The three parameters control three independent factors of the density kernel:

Parameter Factor it controls Role
\(\alpha\) \(x^{\alpha-1}\) shape
\(\beta\) \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\) Gaussian tail
\(\gamma\) \(\exp(\gamma x)\) exponential tilt

Three familiar distributions sit inside the family as exact special cases (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6):

Constraint Reduction
\(\gamma = 0\) \(X^2 \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha/2,\, \beta)\) with rate \(\beta\), i.e. sqrt-Gamma
\(\alpha = 1\) Truncated normal \(\mathrm{TN}(\gamma/(2\beta),\, 1/\sqrt{2\beta},\, 0,\, \infty)\)
\(\alpha = 1,\, \gamma = 0\) Half-normal \(\lvert Z \rvert\) with \(Z \sim N(0,\, 1/(2\beta))\)

rmhn() draws the truncated normal of the second row by the method of Robert (1995).

There is also a degenerate boundary limit, not listed in the table: as \(\beta \to 0^+\) with \(\gamma < 0\), the MHN density converges to \(\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\, -\gamma)\) (Sun et al. 2023, remark after Lemma 6). The package does not handle this limit specially because \(\beta > 0\) is required by the MHN parameter space; for a Gamma draw with \(\beta = 0\), use stats::rgamma directly.

For each of the three finite special cases in the table above — \(\gamma = 0\), \(\alpha = 1\), and both together — the exported functions work through the corresponding standard law — the Gamma law of \(\beta X^2\) for \(\gamma = 0\), the normal law for \(\alpha = 1\) — bypassing the general series-and-rejection machinery. dmhn, pmhn and qmhn do so at those values exactly. A shape or a tilt merely close to them is a different law: at \(\alpha = 1 + \delta\) the log density moves by about \(\delta(\log(\sqrt{\beta}x) - E\log U)\), \(U = \sqrt{\beta}X\), which next to \(x = 10^{-300}\) is about \(10^{-5}\) for \(\delta = 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\), so such a triple takes the general route, which holds its accuracy up to the special values. rmhn draws from the standard laws also where \(|\alpha - 1|\) or the scale-free tilt \(|\gamma|/\sqrt{\beta}\) is below sqrt(.Machine$double.eps): the law drawn is then within a total variation distance of about \(|\delta|\,E|\log U - E\log U|/2\) or \(|z|\,E|U - EU|/2\) of the one requested, and of \(E|\delta L + zV|/2\), with \(L\) and \(V\) those two centred terms, where both are that small and the half-normal is drawn; this is below \(8.6 \times 10^{-9}\), and of Sun et al.’s samplers only Algorithm 2, which the package does not implement (§5.3), covers \(\alpha < 1\) with \(\gamma > 0\), a case method = "sun" would otherwise meet next to \(\alpha = 1\) from below under a positive tilt, and next to \(\gamma = 0\) from above for any \(\alpha < 1\). The one exception to the use of the standard laws is a zero or negligible tilt at a very large shape. The Gamma law then has a relative width of about \(\sqrt{2/\alpha}\), and the rounding of \(\beta x^2\), or of R’s rgamma, would move it by a visible part of that width. So dmhn, pmhn and qmhn use it only up to \(\alpha = 10^6\), beyond which they treat \(\gamma = 0\) like any other tilt (see the last paragraph before §4.1), and rmhn only up to \(\alpha = 2^{60}\), beyond which a rejection sampler placed at the mode takes over (§7).

x  <- seq(0.001, 4, length.out = 400)
plot(x, dmhn(x, alpha = 2,   beta = 1, gamma = 1), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, 1.4), ylab = "f(x)",
     main = "MHN density at beta = 1, gamma = 1")
lines(x, dmhn(x, alpha = 5,   beta = 1, gamma = 1), lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
lines(x, dmhn(x, alpha = 1,   beta = 1, gamma = 1), lwd = 2, col = "tomato")
lines(x, dmhn(x, alpha = 0.5, beta = 1, gamma = 1), lwd = 2, col = "darkorange")
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2,
       col = c("darkorange", "tomato", "black", "steelblue"),
       legend = c("alpha = 0.5  (no interior mode)",
                  "alpha = 1    (truncated normal)",
                  "alpha = 2    (log-concave)",
                  "alpha = 5    (log-concave, shifted right)"))

MHN density as alpha crosses the log-concavity threshold; beta = 1, gamma = 1 fixed.

The figure illustrates the qualitative claims developed in the next section. The density is log-concave whenever \(\alpha \geq 1\) (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 3a). For \(\alpha > 1\) it has a finite interior mode in closed form (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 3b); the borderline case \(\alpha = 1\) reduces to the truncated normal, whose mode is \(\max(0,\, \gamma/(2\beta))\) — interior when \(\gamma > 0\), on the boundary \(x = 0\) otherwise. For \(\alpha < 1\) the density is typically monotone decreasing with a boundary singularity at \(x \to 0^+\). The one exception is \(\gamma > 0\) together with \(\alpha > 1 - \gamma^2/(8\beta)\), where the density is not unimodal: it diverges at \(x \to 0^+\), dips to a local minimum, rises to a single interior local maximum, and then decays (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 3c, which states the condition with \(\geq\); at equality the two stationary points merge into an inflection point and the density is still decreasing). At \((\beta, \gamma) = (1, 1)\) this threshold is \(1 - 1/8 = 0.875\), so the orange (\(\alpha = 0.5\)) curve in the figure sits in the strict monotone-decreasing regime, with no interior local maximum.

Shape and moments

Three facts from Sun et al. (2023) drive everything the package does with shape, moments, and the mode.

Log-concavity is a function of \(\alpha\) alone. For \(\alpha \geq 1\) the density is log-concave irrespective of \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 3a); for \(\alpha < 1\) it is not, because \((\log f)'' = (1 - \alpha)/x^2 - 2\beta\) is positive near \(0\). This threshold is what splits the Gao & Wang (2025) RTDR sampler into its log-axis and original-axis branches in §6 below. Gao & Wang put \(\alpha = 1\) itself on the original axis; the package moves it to the log axis (§6).

The mode has a closed form for \(\alpha > 1\) (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 3b):

\[X_{\mathrm{mode}} = \frac{\gamma + \sqrt{\gamma^2 + 8\beta(\alpha - 1)}}{4\beta}.\]

For \(\alpha = 1\) the mode is \(\max(0,\, \gamma/(2\beta))\) (the truncated-normal mode, Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6b). For \(\gamma \leq 0\) this is the boundary point \(0\). Sun et al. (2023, Lemma 3d) state that no mode exists for \(\gamma < 0\) and \(\alpha \leq 1\); at \(\alpha = 1\) the density is bounded and decreases from its supremum at \(x = 0\), and mhn_mode() returns that point. For \(\alpha < 1\) the density is monotone decreasing unless \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\alpha > 1 - \gamma^2/(8\beta)\), in which case it has a local minimum followed by an interior local maximum (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 3c). Sun et al. (2023, Lemma 3d) state the decrease for \(\gamma < 0\) and for \(\gamma > 0\) with \(\alpha < 1 - \gamma^2/(8\beta)\); at \(\gamma = 0\) the derivative of \(\log f\), \(-(2\beta x^2 + 1 - \alpha)/x\), is negative, and at \(\alpha = 1 - \gamma^2/(8\beta)\) the two stationary points of Lemma 3c merge into an inflection point. The helper mhn_mode() implements this case split. It returns NA for \(\alpha < 1\) without an interior local maximum, and the boundary mode 0 at \(\alpha = 1\) with \(\gamma \leq 0\).

Moments satisfy a two-term recurrence (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 2b):

\[E(X^{k+2}) = \frac{\alpha + k}{2 \beta}\, E(X^{k}) + \frac{\gamma}{2 \beta}\, E(X^{k+1}).\]

Together with the closed-form ratio for \(E(X)\) in terms of \(\Psi\) (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 2a), this gives every higher moment in exact arithmetic. In double precision it does not: central moments formed from raw ones cancel as soon as the standard deviation is small next to the mean, and the ratio of two \(\Psi\) values whose logarithms are each about \(z^2/4\), \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\), loses digits under a strong positive tilt. The helpers therefore use the closed forms only where they are accurate. mhn_mean() takes the Lemma 2a ratio (for \(z\) up to 12, while a bound on its rounding stays small; for \(z < -30\) only below \(\alpha = 6\), and there capped at the upper bound of Sun et al. (2023, Lemma 4a), which holds for every \(\alpha > 0\) by the remark after the lemma), and mhn_var() the Lemma 2c form \(\alpha/(2\beta) + \gamma E(X)/(2\beta) - E(X)^2\) where a bound on its error, from the rounding of its terms and from the error of the mean, stays below \(10^{-8}\) of the result (only for \(z\) between \(-30\) and 12 and, unless \(\gamma = 0\), for \(\alpha\) below 1000). Elsewhere, and for mhn_skewness() and mhn_kurtosis(), the moments are integrated numerically against the density kernel — in the offset from its peak where it has one, and on a logarithmic axis out from the origin where it has none — which needs no \(\Psi\) at all. The Introduction vignette shows the helpers in action. A useful sanity bound (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 4c) is \(\mathrm{Var}(X) \leq 1/(2\beta)\) for every \(\alpha \geq 1\), \(\gamma \in \mathbb{R}\).

The Fox–Wright \(\Psi\) normalising constant

The normalising constant in the MHN density is

\[\Psi\!\left[\frac{\alpha}{2},\, z\right] \;=\; \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\alpha + n}{2}\big)}{n!} \, z^{n}, \qquad z = \frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\beta}}.\]

This series is absolutely convergent for every \(\alpha > 0\) and every \(z \in \mathbb{R}\), and is strictly positive. It depends on \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) only through the two-dimensional combination \((\alpha, z)\).

A useful organisational point: \(\Psi\) matters only for some of the package’s exported functions.

Function group Needs \(\Psi\)? Why
dmhn, pmhn, qmhn yes \(\Psi\) sits in the density’s denominator and in the CDF series.
mhn_mean, mhn_var where accurate \(E(X)\) is the ratio \(\Psi[(\alpha+1)/2,\, z] / (\sqrt{\beta}\,\Psi[\alpha/2,\, z])\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\) follows from it, wherever that is accurate; elsewhere both come from quadrature of the kernel.
mhn_skewness, mhn_kurtosis no The central moments are integrated against the kernel, whose normalising constant cancels from their ratios.
rmhn (Sun or RTDR path) no \(\Psi\) enters both proposal scale and target as a common factor that cancels.

The practical consequence is that any numerical issues in evaluating \(\Psi\) — accumulated rounding in lgamma, or truncation error in the series — can only affect d/p/q and the mean and variance; they cannot leak into the sampler, apart from the weight \(1/(1 + w)\) of the origin that it draws for a subnormal shape (see ?rmhn).

For evaluation, the package uses the closed forms and the series of Sun et al. (2023, Supplementary Lemmas 9 and 10) where they are accurate, and numerical integration elsewhere:

  • At \(z = 0\) exactly \(\Psi[\alpha/2, 0] = \Gamma(\alpha/2)\). A tilt merely close to 0 takes the general route below.
  • At \(\alpha = 1\) exactly, and at \(\alpha = 2\) exactly with \(\gamma > 0\), \(\Psi\) has a closed form involving \(\Phi\) (Sun et al. 2023, Supplementary Lemma 9(c)). For \(\alpha = 1\) under a strong negative tilt (\(z \leq -4\)) it is written through the scaled complementary error function, so that the \(z^2/4\) in its exponent cancels analytically. A shape merely close to 1 or 2 takes the general route below.
  • For \(0 < z \leq 20\) with \(\alpha \leq 100\) the package uses the series of Sun et al. (2023, Supplementary Lemma 10), truncated at an upper bound on the point that lemma gives, or earlier once the terms left can no longer change the sum. All its terms are positive, so there is no catastrophic cancellation.
  • Everywhere else — for \(\gamma < 0\), for \(z > 20\) and for \(\alpha > 100\) — it integrates \(\Psi[\alpha/2, z] = 2\int_0^\infty u^{\alpha-1} e^{-u^2 + z u}\,du\), the normalisation of the density in Sun et al. (2023, Lemma 1a). Past \(z = 20\) the series needs hundreds of terms or more, and the quadrature is both faster and more accurate. Above \(\alpha = 100\) the series is no more accurate than the quadrature and, except at the smallest tilts, where the two take about the same time, slower.

The integral is taken in one of two variables. In either, the integrand is divided by its value at its peak, split there, and cut off where it has fallen by \(L = -\log(\mathrm{tol}) + 40\) below the peak, about 58 at the working tolerance; the panels go to Boost.Math quadrature rules.

  • In \(v = \log u\), for \(z \leq 0\), for \(z > 10^3\), for \(\alpha > 10^6\), and for a shape below 6 whose peak lies within \(\sqrt{L} \approx 7.6\) of the origin. On this axis the integrand is \(u^{\alpha} e^{-u^2 + z u}\), which for either sign of \(z\) has a single analytic peak, at the positive root \(u^{*}\) of \(2u^2 - z u - \alpha = 0\). With \(u = u^{*} e^{w}\), \[\Psi[\alpha/2, z] = 2\, (u^{*})^{\alpha} e^{-(u^{*})^2 + z u^{*}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\!\big(-\alpha(e^{w} - 1 - w) - (u^{*})^2 (e^{w} - 1)^2\big)\,dw.\] Both terms of the exponent are at most 0 and vanish at the peak, so nothing large is subtracted however strong the tilt, and neither the origin nor the power \(u^{\alpha-1}\), whose derivatives are unbounded there, appears. The right side is one 31-point Gauss–Kronrod panel. Far out, the left side falls only like \(\alpha |w|\) — that is the mass \(u^{\alpha-1}\) keeps near the origin — and it is taken on panels \([-2d, -d]\), doubling outwards, until a bound on what remains falls below \(e^{-L}\) of the sum, or until a head next to the origin is reached. That head, below a point \(x_0\) at which \(e^{-u^2 + z u}\) agrees with \(1 + z u - u^2\) to within \(10^{-17}\), is integrated in closed form; it holds most of the mass when \(\alpha\) is tiny — below any representable abscissa once \(\alpha\) is below about \(10^{-3}\).
  • In \(u\), under a positive tilt with \(z \leq 10^3\) and \(\alpha \leq 10^6\) otherwise. The integrand then has an interior peak, near \(z/2\) under a strong tilt, and is a bell about one unit wide there. One 31-point Gauss–Kronrod panel of at most \(\sqrt{L}\) units on each side of the peak integrates it without subdividing (for \(\alpha < 1\) the right panel goes to the double-exponential tanh_sinh rule instead). The range further below the peak is negligible at the working tolerance and is left out, except for a peak nearer the origin than \(\sqrt{L}\) at \(\alpha \geq 6\), where the left panel reaches down to the same closed-form head. In \(u\) the terms \(\alpha \log u\), \(u^2\) and \(z u\) of the exponent, of size \(z^2/4\) and more at the peak, round by more than a panel’s tolerance from \(z\) of a few thousand and from \(\alpha\) near \(10^7\), and the switch to \(\log u\), which forms none of them, comes before that.

The density, distribution and quantile functions need \(\Psi\) only through the difference between its logarithm and the kernel exponent \((\alpha - 1)\log x - \beta x^2 + \gamma x\). Under a strong positive tilt both are about \(z^2/4\) while that difference is of order one, so for \(z > 10^3\) both are formed with \(z^2/4\) removed analytically. For \(\alpha > 10^6\) or \(z > 10^6\), and wherever the terms of the ordinary forms, of size about \(\max(\alpha, z)(1 + |\log v^{*}|)\), grow past \(10^7\), dmhn, pmhn and qmhn measure the law instead from the peak \(v^{*} = u^{*}/\sqrt{\beta}\) of the density of \(\log X\), the positive root of \(2\beta x^2 - \gamma x - \alpha = 0\), and normalise it by the integral over \(w\) above. The two tails are then integrals of the same integrand over the two sides of \(w = \log(q / v^{*})\), and nothing of the size of \(\alpha \log x\) or \(z^2/4\) is formed. \(v^{*}\) is held as a double next to it plus its offset from that double, so that the offset of \(x\) from the peak is exact even where the law is narrower than the spacing of the doubles near its peak. The help pages of these functions state the range over which the results are accurate.

Errata in Sun et al. (2023)

The published paper has six typesetting errors in results this vignette draws on that affect what is computed from them: four in the main text (two in Theorem 1, one in Lemma 7 and one in step 2 of Algorithm 3) and two in its Supplementary Material (the statement of Lemma 10, and the curvature \(l''\) in Section 2.17). The paper has other slips in the results cited, which do not. In each of the six cases the paper itself carries the correct form elsewhere — in a proof, in a neighbouring display, or in the expression being differentiated — and the package uses the correct form.

  • Square-root-of-Gamma density and selection rule in Theorem 1. Theorem 1 gives the density of the square root of a Gamma variable as \(f_{\sqrt{\mathrm{Gam}}}(x \mid \alpha, \delta) = x^{\alpha-1}\delta^{\alpha/2}e^{-\delta x^{2}}/\Gamma(\alpha/2)\), which integrates to \(1/2\); the density is twice that, and the constant \(K_{2}\) of its first part is the one for the density with the factor 2. The indicator that picks the proposal is printed as \(I = \mathbb{I}(K_{1}(\delta, \alpha, \beta, \gamma) \le K_{2}(\mu, \alpha, \beta, \gamma))\), with the first arguments of \(K_{1}\) and \(K_{2}\) exchanged: \(K_{1}\) is a function of \(\mu\) and \(K_{2}\) of \(\delta\), as Algorithm 1 uses them. (The theorem also labels two of its parts “a”.) The package draws the proposal as the square root of a Gamma variate, whose density carries the factor 2, and compares \(K_{1}(\mu_{\mathrm{opt}}, \cdot)\) with \(K_{2}(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}, \cdot)\).

  • Mixture weights \(p_{i}\) in Lemma 7. The main-text statement of Lemma 7 gives the weights for the \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Gamma}}\) mixture representation as \(p_{i} = \tfrac{1}{2\beta^{\alpha/2}} \cdot \tfrac{\Gamma((\alpha + i)/2)\, (\gamma/\sqrt{\beta})^{i}} {i!\, \Psi[\alpha/2,\, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]}\). By the definition of \(\Psi\) these sum to \(1/(2\beta^{\alpha/2})\) rather than one, contradicting the Poisson–Gamma hierarchical representation in Sun et al. (2023, Lemma 5a). The correct form, reproduced in the supplementary proof of Lemma 7 (Supplementary Section 2.13), is \[p_{i} \;=\; \frac{\Gamma((\alpha + i)/2)\, (\gamma/\sqrt{\beta})^{i}} {i!\, \Psi[\alpha/2,\, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]}\] i.e. drop the leading \(1/(2\beta^{\alpha/2})\). This affects Algorithm 2 only, which the package does not implement; the correction is recorded here for completeness.

  • Series truncation discriminants \(C_{1}\), \(C_{2}\) in Lemma 10. Lemma 10 (Supplementary Section 1) splits the series for \(\Psi[\alpha/2, x]\) into its even and odd terms, \(A(k)\) and \(B(k)\). Its parts (a) and (b) give indices \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) beyond which the ratio of successive terms, \(A(k+1)/A(k)\) or \(B(k+1)/B(k)\), stays below a fixed contraction factor \(q \in (0, 1)\), and part (d) sets the truncation point \(K = \max\{K_{1}, K_{2}\}\) for a tolerance \(\epsilon\) at the indices, no smaller than \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\), past which every term is at most \(\epsilon/4\); the package truncates at the upper bound on them that the geometric decay gives. Reducing the ratio bound to a quadratic in \(k\) gives a discriminant whose last term is \(\alpha x^{2}\) (and \((\alpha+1) x^{2}\) for \(C_{2}\)). The statement of Lemma 10 prints these as \(\alpha x\) and \((\alpha+1) x\) — a single missing power of \(x\). Its proof (Supplementary Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2) carries \(z^{2}\) throughout, in agreement with the rederivation. The corrected \(x^{2}\) form, with \(q = 1/2\), is what the package uses in src/mhn_psi_series.cpp (marked with an // ERRATA comment). With the printed form, \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) can fall below the index from which the ratio is actually at most \(q\), so the geometric tail bound of part (d) no longer follows. Under the package’s truncation rule the effect on the computed \(\Psi\) is negligible; the corrected form is used because it is the one the proof supports.

  • Gamma shape in step 2 of Algorithm 3. Algorithm 3 proposes \(X = m T^{r}\) with \(r = (\beta m + |\gamma|)/(2\beta m + |\gamma|)\). The display that introduces it gives the Gamma shape of \(T\) as \(\alpha(\beta m + |\gamma|)/(2\beta m + |\gamma|) = \alpha r\), which makes \(X\) follow the proposal kernel of Theorem 3; step 2 prints it as \((\beta m + |\gamma|\alpha)/(2\beta m + |\gamma|)\), with the parentheses lost. The two agree only at \(\alpha = 1\), and with the printed shape the acceptance test of step 5 would no longer return MHN draws. The package uses \(\alpha r\). The same display sets \(Y = T^{r}\), whose density matches the kernel of Theorem 3 only at \(m = 1\); step 3’s \(X = m T^{r}\), which the package draws, matches it for every \(m\).

  • Sign in the curvature \(l''\) of Supplementary Section 2.17. The Newton–Raphson refinement of the Algorithm 3 matching point uses the first two derivatives of the log acceptance probability \(l(m)\). Differentiating the printed \(l'\) gives a first term \(-4\alpha\beta^{2}|\gamma|/(2\beta m + |\gamma|)^{3}\) times \(\psi(\alpha(\beta m + |\gamma|)/(2\beta m + |\gamma|)) - \log(\beta m^{2} + m|\gamma|)\); the printed \(l''\) has it with a plus sign. At the starting point \(m_{\mathrm{init}}\) that changes the length of the Newton step: at \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = (3, 1, -2)\), with \(m_{\mathrm{init}} = 0.772\), \(l''\) is \(-1.03\) and the printed form gives \(-1.17\). Farther from it the printed curvature can take the wrong sign, which reverses the step: at \((2, 1, -0.1)\) and \(m = 0.223\), \(l''\) is \(-20.9\) and the printed form gives \(+1.9\). The package uses the minus sign.

Sampling: Sun et al. (2023)

Sun et al. (2023) propose three Accept–Reject schemes, indexed by the sign of \(\gamma\) and a coarse split on \(\alpha\). Two of them — Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 3 — are implemented in the package and reachable via rmhn(method = "sun"). Algorithm 2 is not, and this section explains the reason.

Algorithm 1 — \(\gamma > 0\), \(\alpha > 1\)

For each parameter triple, Algorithm 1 constructs two proposal distributions — a Normal with mean \(\mu_{\mathrm{opt}}\) and variance \(1/(2\beta)\), and a \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha/2,\, \delta_{\mathrm{opt}})}\) — each with a multiplicative envelope constant \(K_{1}\) and \(K_{2}\). Setup chooses whichever envelope is tighter (\(K_{1} \leq K_{2}\) or the reverse). The two optima \(\mu_{\mathrm{opt}}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}\) have closed forms (Sun et al. 2023, Theorem 1), so setup is cheap. The acceptance probability is bounded below by 0.8 for \(\alpha \geq 4\) (Sun et al. 2023, Theorem 2e). Above \(\alpha = 10^{18}\) the package takes the Normal proposal whatever the constants of Theorem 1: R’s Gamma generator builds its variate from \(\sqrt{\alpha/2 - 1/2}\) rounded to double precision, which would shift the square-root-of-Gamma proposal by an amount the acceptance test cannot see (§7). Under a small tilt the Normal proposal accepts about \(1/\sqrt{2}\) of its proposals there (0.706 at \(\alpha = 2 \times 10^{18}\)), below that bound, and the law drawn stays exact. For \(1 \leq \alpha < 4\) no uniform lower bound is proved, but Figure 2 of Sun et al. (2023), computed numerically, shows high acceptance throughout that range.

Algorithm 3 — \(\gamma \leq 0\)

When the tilt is non-positive, Theorem 3 of Sun et al. (2023) supplies a proposal kernel based on an AM–GM-type inequality. (Sun et al. print Algorithm 3 for \(\gamma < 0\), Theorem 4 and Figure 4 for \(\gamma \leq 0\); at \(\gamma = 0\) the package uses the square-root-Gamma closed form.) With a tuning point \(m > 0\) and the exponent \(r = (\beta m + |\gamma|)/(2\beta m + |\gamma|)\), the candidate is

\[T \sim \mathrm{Gamma}\!\big(\alpha \cdot r,\, m(\beta m + |\gamma|)\big), \qquad X = m \cdot T^{r}.\]

The construction works for every \(\alpha > 0\); the package uses it up to \(\alpha = 2^{59}\), beyond which the rounding of R’s rgamma would shift its proposals alike by more than a few times \(10^{-7}\) of a standard deviation (§7). For \(\alpha > 1\), Sun et al. (2023, Theorem 4c) prove an acceptance probability of at least \(1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707\) (the theorem is stated for \(\alpha > 1\); its proof in the Supplementary Material treats \(\alpha \geq 3\)) at the optimal matching point and at the explicit point \(m_{\star} = (\gamma + \sqrt{\gamma^{2} + 8\alpha\beta})/(4\beta)\); for \(\alpha \leq 1\) the procedure still samples correctly, but no bound is proved. The matching point is initialised from a heuristic adapted from Sun et al. (2023, Section 4.2): \(m_{\mathrm{init}} = \alpha^{2}/\{(1 + \alpha)\sqrt{\beta}\}\) for \(\alpha \leq 1.1\) (Sun et al. print \(\alpha^{2}/(1+\alpha)\), which is the same point at \(\beta = 1\); the package divides by \(\sqrt{\beta}\) so that the matching point scales with \(X\), since \(\sqrt{\beta}X \sim \mathrm{MHN}(\alpha, 1, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta})\)), and a combination of the mode and the rightmost inflection point for \(\alpha > 1.1\) (the inflection point is a quartic root, which the package locates by bisection). The package then applies a single Newton-Raphson refinement step in both regimes, producing \(m_{\mathrm{recommend}}\), whose acceptance probability is within 0.002 of the optimum across the parameter range tabulated in Sun et al. (2023, Table 1). For this matching point the \(1/\sqrt{2}\) level is observed, not proved. Past a tilt \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta} = 10^{150}\), where the law is its \(\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha, -\gamma)\) limit to double precision, the matching point for \(\alpha \leq 1.1\) is simply the mean \(\alpha/|\gamma|\) of that limit, without a Newton step.

Why Algorithm 2 is not implemented

Algorithm 2 targets \(\gamma > 0\) with \(\alpha < 1\) via the mixture representation

\[f_{\mathrm{MHN}}(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} p_{i}\, f_{i}(x \mid \alpha, \beta), \qquad f_{i} \;\sim\; \sqrt{\mathrm{Gamma}\!\big((\alpha + i)/2,\, \beta\big)}.\]

The mixture-index sampler keeps the first \(M+1\) weights and bounds the rest by a geometric envelope, which needs \(M \geq M^{\dagger} = \max\{\lfloor\alpha\rfloor, \lfloor\gamma^{2}/(\varepsilon_{1}^{2}\beta)\rfloor\}\), the point beyond which successive weights shrink by at least a factor \(\varepsilon_{1}\) (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 8). With \(\varepsilon_{1} = 1/2\), as in their example, \(M^{\dagger} = \lfloor 4\gamma^{2}/\beta\rfloor\) for \(\alpha < 1\), so for large \(\gamma^{2}/\beta\) the whole scheme degrades catastrophically — Gao & Wang (2025, Table 1) report a slowdown of up to \(\sim 3 \times 10^{4}\times\) against RTDR in the most extreme case \((\alpha, \gamma) = (0.01, 10000)\). The package therefore declines to implement Algorithm 2 and routes \((\alpha < 1, \gamma > 0)\) to RTDR, whose acceptance Gao & Wang (2025) bound below by \(1/e\) (next section).

Sampling: Gao & Wang (2025) RTDR

Gao & Wang (2025) introduce a Relaxed Transformed Density Rejection (RTDR) sampler that comes with a uniform lower bound on the acceptance probability across the entire parameter space.

Gao & Wang (2025) write the density as proportional to \(x^{\lambda-1}\exp(-\alpha x^{2}-\beta x)\): their \((\lambda, \alpha, \beta)\) are the package’s \((\alpha, \beta, -\gamma)\), so their \(\beta < 2(\sqrt{1-2\lambda}-1)\) reads \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta} > 2(1-\sqrt{1-2\alpha})\) here. Below, the symbols are the package’s. Three ideas drive the construction.

\(T_{c}\)-concavity

Standard TDR builds piecewise-linear envelopes on top of a log-transformed density. RTDR generalises to the \(T_{c}\) family

\[T_{c}[x] = \mathrm{sign}(c) \cdot x^{c} \quad (c > -1,\, c \neq 0), \qquad T_{0}[x] = \log x.\]

A density \(f\) is \(T_{c}\)-concave if \(T_{c}[f]\) is concave. Logarithmic concavity (the usual TDR setting) is the \(c = 0\) special case. In regions (b) and (c) below, which transform the package’s RTDR implementation uses on the log-axis density turns on the sign of the tilt: for \(\gamma > 0\) it takes \(c = -1/2\), because \(\log g\) is then convex on \((-\infty, \log(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}/4))\) and a log-tangent hat would fail to dominate there, while \(T_{-1/2}[x] = -x^{-1/2}\) still does. For \(\gamma \leq 0\) the log-axis density is log-concave and the ordinary \(c = 0\) tangent hat is used. In region (d), \(g\) is in general not \(T_{-1/2}\)-concave, and the envelope of Gao & Wang (2025, Section 4) is used instead.

Working on the log axis when \(\alpha < 1\)

When \(\alpha < 1\) the density \(f(x \mid \alpha, \gamma)\) on \((0, \infty)\) blows up at the left endpoint and is not amenable to direct envelope construction. The change of variable \(y = \log x\) yields

\[g(y \mid \alpha, \gamma) \;=\; \exp\!\big( \alpha y - e^{2y} + \gamma e^{y} \big), \qquad y \in \mathbb{R},\]

which is bounded and unimodal (Gao & Wang 2025, Lemma 3.3). Gao & Wang’s RTDR operates on \(g\) for \(\alpha < 1\) and on \(f\) directly for \(\alpha \geq 1\); the package moves \(\alpha = 1\) itself to \(g\), so that it works on \(g\) for \(\alpha \leq 1\) and on \(f\) for \(\alpha > 1\) (see region (b) below).

The four regions

After scale normalisation \(\sqrt{\beta} X \to X\) (so we may assume \(\beta = 1\)), the RTDR envelope construction splits into four regions based on \((\alpha, \gamma)\). The \(\gamma\) in the table below is the normalised tilt \(\gamma_{\mathrm{norm}} = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\); for a general \(\beta\) the package’s rmhn(method = "rtdr") rescales internally and compares \(\gamma_{\mathrm{norm}}\) against the boundary \(2(1 - \sqrt{1 - 2\alpha})\).

Region \(\alpha\) \(\gamma\) Envelope target Reference
(a) \(> 1\) \(^{\dagger}\) any \(f\) log-concave Gao & Wang (2025, Theorem 3.1)
(b) \([1/2,\, 1]\) \(^{\dagger}\) any \(g\) log-concave if \(\gamma \leq 0\), else \(T_{-1/2}\)-concave Gao & Wang (2025, Corollary 3.1; Theorem 3.2)
(c) \((0,\, 1/2)\) \(\leq 2(1 - \sqrt{1 - 2\alpha})\) \(g\) log-concave if \(\gamma \leq 0\), else \(T_{-1/2}\)-concave Gao & Wang (2025, Lemma 3.5; Theorem 3.2)
(d) \((0,\, 1/2)\) \(> 2(1 - \sqrt{1 - 2\alpha})\) \(g\) with inflection at \(y^{*} = \log(\gamma/4)\) Gao & Wang (2025, Theorem 4.4)

\(^{\dagger}\) The boundary between (a) and (b) is the package’s: Gao & Wang (2025) put \(\alpha = 1\) in region (a).

Region (a) is the easiest: \(f\) is log-concave, and two tangent lines and a constant segment suffice (Gao & Wang 2025, Eq. (11)); for \(\alpha \le e\) and \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta} \le \sqrt{8\{\sqrt{(e-1)(\alpha-1)}-(\alpha-1)\}}\) the left tangent is dropped and the constant runs from 0 (their Eq. (10)). Gao & Wang put the boundary \(\alpha = 1\) in region (a) (their Theorem 3.1, and if(lambda >= 1) in the R code of their Appendix B). The package handles it in region (b) instead, which their Theorem 3.2 also covers (\(g\) is \(T_{-1/2}\)-concave for \(\alpha \geq 1/2\)): \(f\) is log-concave at \(\alpha = 1\) too, but the envelope of region (a) is built around an interior mode in \(x\), and at \(\alpha = 1\) with \(\gamma \leq 0\) the density’s maximum is at the boundary \(x = 0\), not at an interior mode. On the log axis \(g\) has a finite mode for every \(\alpha > 0\) (its \(x = e^{y}\) is positive), so the region (b) construction applies without a special case. Regions (b) and (c) share one construction on \(g\); the sign of \(\gamma\) picks the transform. Since \(\mathrm{d}^{2} \log g / \mathrm{d} y^{2} = \gamma e^{y} - 4 e^{2y}\) is negative for every \(y\) exactly when \(\gamma \leq 0\), a \(T_0\) log-tangent hat serves on that side, while for \(\gamma > 0\) only \(T_{-1/2}\)-concavity survives and the hat switches to inverse-square pieces. Region (d) is the hardest — \(g\) has an inflection point, and the envelope adds a chain of secant segments on the log-convex side. In the envelope of Gao & Wang (2025, Eqs. (14)-(15)), which their Theorem 4.4 validates, \(K = \lceil\rho\rceil\) breakpoints sit on that side, and \(\rho\) grows roughly linearly in \(\gamma\) (\(K = 127909\) at \(\gamma = 10^{5}\)). When the envelope has a left tangent line, the package stops the chain as soon as a breakpoint falls below it, the test used in the R code of their Appendix B; without one, which happens only for \(\gamma\) below about 6.3, \(\lceil\rho\rceil\) is at most eight. So only a handful of breakpoints is ever built, and just one once \(\gamma\) exceeds about 32. Their Eq. (15) prints the left-tangent interval as \((y^{*}, p_l)\), leaving \((\dot t_l, y^{*}]\) uncovered, where \(\dot t_l < y^{*}\) is the point at which \(\log g\) has the slope of the tangent at \(t_l\); the package follows their Theorem 4.3, \((\dot t_l, p_l]\), and like their Appendix B code starts the tangent at the last breakpoint kept.

Why “relaxed”

The classical TDR construction asks for optimal tangent contact points, which generally have no closed form and must be found by Newton iteration. Gao & Wang (2025, Corollary 2.1 and Eq. (7)) show that the rejection constant stays \(\leq e \approx 2.718\) (equivalently, acceptance probability \(\geq 1/e \approx 0.368\)) as long as the contact points lie anywhere inside a fixed interval — namely

\[\log\!\frac{f(m)}{f(t)} \in \begin{cases} [0.46,\, 2.49] & f \text{ log-concave (region (a))}, \\ [0.46,\, 2.49] & g \text{ log-concave (regions (b), (c), } \gamma \leq 0), \\ [0.93,\, 1.99] & g \text{ $T_{-1/2}$-concave (regions (b), (c), } \gamma > 0). \end{cases}\]

Setup is therefore a handful of cheap iterations that terminate as soon as the bracket is hit, with no need for a precise Newton solution. This is why Gao & Wang (2025) call the setup fast: compared with classical TDR, which must solve for optimal contact points, or with generic methods such as adaptive rejection sampling and numerical inversion, it suits varying-parameter settings such as a Gibbs sampler, where \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) changes every iteration and each setup serves a single draw. They make no such claim against Sun et al. (2023), whose generator they find comparable for \(\gamma < 0\) or \(\alpha > 1\) (their Section 5). Algorithm 1’s setup costs less than RTDR’s, so method = "auto" keeps it for single draws with \(\gamma > 0\), \(\alpha > 1\), and §7 explains how it splits both signs of \(\gamma\) between the Sun algorithms and RTDR by batch size and, for \(\gamma > 0\), by tilt. RTDR’s own advantages are a lighter per-proposal cost, which wins every large \(\gamma < 0\) batch and the large \(\gamma > 0\) batches at mild tilt (§7), and the \(1/e\) bound below; it is also the package’s only sampler for \(\alpha < 1\), \(\gamma > 0\).

Composing the bounds of Gao & Wang (2025) — Theorem 3.1 for region (a), Corollary 2.1 with Eq. (7) for regions (b) and (c), whose concavity their Theorem 3.2 establishes, and Theorem 4.4 for region (d) — yields the headline guarantee of RTDR: for every \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) with \(\alpha > 0\), \(\beta > 0\), \(\gamma \in \mathbb{R}\), the acceptance probability of their construction is at least \(1/e \approx 0.368\), provided its contact points lie in the band of their Eq. (7). The package’s search for those points does not always reach that band (see ?rmhn), and the acceptance measured stays above \(1/e\) there too. Sun et al.’s (2023) bounds are uniform only on parts of the parameter space: at least 0.8 for Algorithm 1 when \(\alpha \geq 4\) (Theorem 2e), at least \(1/\sqrt{2}\) for Algorithm 3 when \(\alpha > 1\) at the optimal matching point \(m_{\mathrm{opt}}\) and at \(m_{\star}\) (Theorem 4c; the package’s one-step Newton \(m\) is not covered), and none for Algorithm 2 (§5).

A quick sanity check that the RTDR sampler converges to the right distribution in all four regions — empirical means from RTDR vs theoretical means across regions (a), (b), (c), (d), each based on 5000 draws:

cases <- data.frame(
  region = c("(a)", "(b)", "(c)", "(d)"),
  alpha  = c(2.0,    0.7,    0.3,    0.3),
  gamma  = c(0.5,    1.0,    0.5,    5.0)
)
set.seed(42)
empirical <- mapply(
  function(a, g) mean(rmhn(5000, alpha = a, beta = 1, gamma = g, method = "rtdr")),
  cases$alpha, cases$gamma
)
theoretical <- mapply(mhn_mean, cases$alpha, beta = 1, cases$gamma)
data.frame(cases,
           empirical_mean   = round(empirical,   4),
           theoretical_mean = round(theoretical, 4))
#>   region alpha gamma empirical_mean theoretical_mean
#> 1    (a)   2.0   0.5         1.0126           1.0016
#> 2    (b)   0.7   1.0         0.6468           0.6424
#> 3    (c)   0.3   0.5         0.2931           0.2823
#> 4    (d)   0.3   5.0         2.3300           2.3221

The four rows hit the right means to within about two Monte-Carlo standard errors — at \(n = 5000\) those errors run from \(0.005\) to \(0.011\), so the gaps land in the second decimal place, not the third.

The rmhn(method = "auto") dispatch

rmhn exposes three values of method: "sun" (the Sun Algorithm 1 / 3 path), "rtdr" (the Gao & Wang RTDR path), and "auto" (default). The first two select the sampler used for the general case; the closed-form special cases below are taken first whatever method is set to, since they are exact and need next to no setup. The "auto" route is the package’s recommendation; it combines the special cases and the three samplers into one decision tree, whose ordinary thresholds come from timing the samplers against each other:

                  rmhn(n, alpha, beta, gamma, method = "auto")
                                    │
                                    ▼
       ┌─ alpha = 1, gamma = 0  →  half-normal       (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6c)
       │
       ├─ gamma = 0             →  sqrt-Gamma        (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6a)
       │      (above alpha = 2^60: the Normal proposal of Sun Algorithm 1)
       │
       ├─ alpha = 1             →  truncated normal  (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6b)
       │
       ├─ alpha < 1 and gamma > 0
       │      →  RTDR  (regions (b) / (c) / (d), Gao & Wang 2025, Theorems 3.2, 4.4)
       │
       ├─ alpha > 1 and gamma > 0
       │      ├─ alpha ≤ 2^59, gamma / sqrt(beta) ≤ 2 sqrt(alpha),
       │      │  samples_per_setup ≥ N+         →  RTDR    (region (a))
       │      └─ otherwise                      →  Sun Algorithm 1
       │                                           (Sun et al. 2023, Theorems 1, 2)
       │         where N+, for gamma / sqrt(beta) ≤ sqrt(alpha) / above it, is
       │           5 / 25  (alpha < 10),          25 / 50   (10 ≤ alpha < 1e3),
       │          50 / 100 (1e3 ≤ alpha < 1e8),  100 / 1000 (alpha ≥ 1e8),
       │         and 5 / 25 where RTDR's setup starts next to the mode (*)
       │
       └─ gamma < 0
              ├─ alpha > 2^59                   →  RTDR
              ├─ -gamma / sqrt(beta) > 1e150    →  Sun Algorithm 3
              ├─ alpha < 2.5e-324 * (-gamma / sqrt(beta))
              │      →  Sun Algorithm 3  (the log-axis mode rounds to 0)
              ├─ samples_per_setup ≥ N*, or RTDR's setup
              │  starts next to the mode (*)    →  RTDR    (regions (a)-(c))
              └─ otherwise                      →  Sun Algorithm 3
                 where N* = 25 for alpha < 0.1, 5 for 0.1 ≤ alpha < 1,
                 1 for 1 < alpha < 1e3, 10 for 1e3 ≤ alpha < 1e5,
                 25 for 1e5 ≤ alpha < 1e8, 50 for alpha ≥ 1e8

  (*) region (a), alpha > 1: gamma / sqrt(beta) < -1e10 sqrt(alpha), or the
      centred construction, from a shape of about 2.4e12 to 3.1e12 at
      moderate tilts, of about 2.3e13 near a tilt of -alpha / e and of
      about 4.5e13 at any tilt

Write \(S\) for the samples_per_setup quantity that the branches above compare with \(N^{+}\) and \(N^{*}\),

\[S \;=\; \begin{cases} n, & L_{\alpha} = L_{\beta} = L_{\gamma} = 1, \\ \lfloor n / P \rfloor, & 2 \le P \le 256 \text{ and } 4P \le n, \\ 1, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}\]

where \(L_{\alpha}\), \(L_{\beta}\), \(L_{\gamma}\) are the lengths of the three parameter vectors and \(P = \operatorname{lcm}(L_{\alpha}, L_{\beta}, L_{\gamma})\) is the period after which the recycled triples repeat. In the middle case rmhn keeps a setup for each position within the period, and each serves \(\lfloor n/P \rfloor\) draws; otherwise consecutive draws may need different setups, and a call with parameter vectors of length \(n\) counts one draw per setup, as the loop of single draws in a Gibbs sampler does. The intuition follows from decomposing the expected time per draw as

\[E[\text{time}/\text{draw}] \;=\; \frac{T_{\text{setup}}}{S} \;+\; C_{\text{reject}} \times T_{\text{per-proposal}},\]

where \(T_{\text{setup}}\) is the one-off cost of preparing the proposal (the \(m_{\text{init}}\) heuristic plus at most one Newton step for Sun Algorithm 3; an iterative contact-point search for RTDR), \(C_{\text{reject}} = 1/\text{acceptance}\) is the expected number of proposals per accepted draw, and \(T_{\text{per-proposal}}\) is the cost of one proposal cycle (sample plus acceptance log-ratio evaluation).

For \(\gamma < 0\) and \(\alpha < 1\) the two samplers sit on opposite ends of this trade-off:

  • Sun Algorithm 3 has a cheap setup — \(m_{\text{init}}\) is explicit for \(\alpha \leq 1.1\) and needs one bisection for the inflection point above that, and the single Newton refinement uses two boost::math::digamma evaluations and one boost::math::trigamma — but a more expensive per-proposal: every proposal calls rgamma and evaluates the fractional power \(X = m \cdot T^{r}\). The acceptance log-ratio reuses \(T = (X/m)^{1/r}\) directly. Its three terms are each of the order of the Gamma rate \(R\) and cancel to order one, so above \(R = 10^{6}\), where their rounding would no longer be negligible, it is evaluated in the form \(R\,w\,[(1+v)^{p} - 1 - p v]\), with \(w = X/m\), \(v = w - 1\) and \(p = \beta m/(\beta m + |\gamma|)\).
  • RTDR (region (a)) has a more expensive setup: each contact point \(t_{l}\), \(t_{r}\) is found by an iterative search that terminates as soon as \(\log f(m)/f(t)\) lands in the bracket \([0.46,\, 2.49]\). The search starts from \(m/2\) and \(m + \max(1, m/2)\) — not from \(m \mp \sqrt{-2/(\log f)''(m)}\), which Gao & Wang (2025) recommend after their Eq. (8) and use throughout the R code of their Appendix B — and walks in, in about \(\log_2 m\) Newton steps, except where the construction is centred at the mode (once the magnitudes of the three terms of \(\log f(m)\), which set the scale of its rounding error, sum past \(0.01\) divided by the machine epsilon: from a shape of about \(2.4 \times 10^{12}\) to \(3.1 \times 10^{12}\) at moderate tilts, of about \(2.3 \times 10^{13}\) near a tilt of \(-\alpha/e\), and of about \(4.5 \times 10^{13}\) at any tilt) or \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) is below \(-10^{10}\sqrt{\alpha}\); there it starts next to the mode, at the offset that Gao & Wang (2025, Section 2) recommend. But the per-proposal is light: sampling from the piecewise envelope is straight arithmetic plus a single log, and the acceptance ratio adds only two more logs.

When \(S\) is large the per-proposal term dominates and RTDR wins; when it is small — the Gibbs case where each iteration redraws \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) — the setup term does. The crossovers come from two paired timing races of the two samplers, whose scripts and results are not shipped with the package, and from three runs of inst/benchmarks/auto_dispatch.R (installed at system.file("benchmarks", "auto_dispatch.R", package = "mhn")), whose grid starts at \(\alpha = 0.3\); all were timed on an Apple M1 Ultra, and the crossings move from machine to machine. The first race covers \(\alpha\) from 0.01 to \(10^4\) and \(|\gamma|/\sqrt{\beta}\) from 0.5 to \(10^4\); the second covers shapes from \(10^3\) to \(10^{14}\) under tilts of both signs, positive tilts from 1.25 to 3 times \(\sqrt{\alpha\beta}\) at shapes from 1.5 to 1000, and single draws within one vectorised call, which pays a setup per draw without R’s cost per call. For \(\gamma < 0\) Algorithm 3 wins single draws for \(\alpha < 1\) (by 11–23% at \(\alpha = 0.01\), by at most 2% for \(\alpha\) from 0.3 to 0.8), and RTDR takes over from \(S = 5\), or \(S = 25\) at \(\alpha = 0.01\), where the spike at the origin makes Algorithm 3’s setup relatively cheapest. For \(\alpha > 1\) Algorithm 3 locates its matching point by bisection and Newton steps, and RTDR wins at every \(S\) from \(\alpha = 1.5\) to 100. From \(\alpha = 10^3\), where RTDR’s search walks in, its setup is the dearer: Algorithm 3 wins single draws, RTDR taking up to 1.4 times as long, and up to 5.2 times in a vectorised call, and RTDR takes over from \(S = 5\) or 10 at \(\alpha = 10^3\), 10 or 25 at \(10^4\), 25 or 50 from \(10^5\) to \(10^8\) and 50 beyond. Where its search starts next to the mode, RTDR wins at every \(S\), single draws included (by 3.5–5%, and by 16–33% in a vectorised call). For \(\gamma > 0\), \(\alpha > 1\) Algorithm 1 wins or ties single draws at every shape and tilt timed (RTDR takes 1.6 to 13 times as long in a vectorised call), and its per-proposal cost depends on \(\gamma/\sqrt{\alpha\beta}\). Up to about 1 it proposes from the square root of a Gamma law, one rgamma call per proposal, and RTDR wins from \(S = 5\) (\(\alpha \le 5\)), 10 (\(\alpha = 10\)), 25 (\(\alpha = 100\)), 25 or 50 (\(\alpha\) from \(10^3\) to \(10^8\)) or 50 to 200 (\(\alpha = 10^{10}\) and \(10^{12}\)), by up to 72%. Above it, up to 2, Algorithm 1 proposes from a Normal law that accepts only 0.81–0.92 of its proposals, and RTDR still wins large batches, from a larger \(S\) and by up to 14% (34% at \(\alpha = 10^7\), where Algorithm 1’s acceptance test is dear). From about 2.5–3 on Algorithm 1 wins nearly every \(S\): beyond 2, RTDR gains at most 3.4% at shapes up to 1000 and 1.4% at larger ones, but 13% at \(\alpha = 10^7\). The rule cuts at \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta} = 2\sqrt{\alpha}\) and splits its thresholds at \(\sqrt{\alpha}\), near Algorithm 1’s own switch of proposal (at the tilt \(\Delta_{\mathrm{crit}} \geq \sqrt{\alpha}\) where \(K_{1} = K_{2}\), with \(\Delta_{\mathrm{crit}}/\sqrt{\alpha} \to 1\) as \(\alpha \to \infty\); Sun et al. 2023, Section 4.1.1): 5 and 25 below \(\alpha = 10\), 25 and 50 up to \(10^3\), 50 and 100 up to \(10^8\), 100 and 1000 beyond, and 5 and 25 where RTDR’s search starts next to the mode.

The remaining branches come from the limits of double precision, and ordinary parameters never reach them. R’s rgamma rounds \(\sqrt{a - 1/2}\) and the scale of a Gamma variate of shape \(a\), and so shifts every variate alike by up to about \(3 \times 2^{-53}\sqrt{a}\) of its standard deviation; Algorithm 3’s own setup, which rounds the proposal’s shape, power and rate, adds a shift of the same order. The package keeps such common shifts to a few times \(10^{-7}\) of a standard deviation. So the sqrt-Gamma closed form is used only up to \(\alpha = 2^{60}\), a Gamma shape of \(2^{59}\), and Algorithm 3 only up to \(\alpha = 2^{59}\); beyond, the draws are placed from the mode computed to about twice double precision, at any batch size: by the Normal proposal of Algorithm 1, centred at the mode, for a zero or negligible tilt of either sign (\(|\gamma|/\sqrt{\beta}\) below sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)), and by RTDR for any other \(\gamma < 0\). Sun et al. state Algorithm 1 for \(\gamma > 0\) and Theorem 1 for \(\gamma \geq 0\), but centred at the mode the Normal envelope holds for either sign. A positive tilt goes to Algorithm 1 above \(\alpha = 2^{59}\), also at any batch size: no timing reaches that far, and RTDR cannot represent the law from a shape of about \(10^{31}\) on (from between \(2^{103}\) and \(2^{106}\), see ?rmhn), while Algorithm 1 draws it. Past a tilt \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta} = 10^{150}\) Algorithm 3 proposes the \(\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha, -\gamma)\) limit of the law itself and accepts practically every proposal, at a setup cost no envelope construction can undercut, so it is used there at any batch size. And where RTDR cannot place the law at all — for \(\alpha \le 1\) it works with \(\log(\sqrt{\beta} X)\), whose mode is the logarithm of about \(\alpha\sqrt{\beta}/|\gamma|\), and below a shape of about \(2.5 \times 10^{-324}\,|\gamma|/\sqrt{\beta}\) that number rounds to 0 — Algorithm 3 is used as well, under method = "rtdr" too.

A small concrete demonstration: with set.seed aligned, method = "auto" and the expected forced method produce bit-identical draws on each branch.

# Branch: alpha < 1 and gamma > 0  -->  expects RTDR
set.seed(7); auto1 <- rmhn(20, alpha = 0.7, beta = 1, gamma = 2)
set.seed(7); rtdr1 <- rmhn(20, alpha = 0.7, beta = 1, gamma = 2, method = "rtdr")
identical(auto1, rtdr1)
#> [1] TRUE

# Branch: alpha > 1, gamma > 2 sqrt(alpha beta)  -->  expects Sun Algorithm 1
set.seed(7); auto2 <- rmhn(20, alpha = 3,   beta = 1, gamma = 5)
set.seed(7); sun2  <- rmhn(20, alpha = 3,   beta = 1, gamma = 5, method = "sun")
identical(auto2, sun2)
#> [1] TRUE

# Branch: alpha > 1, gamma <= sqrt(alpha beta), 5 or more draws per setup
#   -->  expects RTDR
set.seed(7); auto3 <- rmhn(20, alpha = 3,   beta = 1, gamma = 1.5)
set.seed(7); rtdr3 <- rmhn(20, alpha = 3,   beta = 1, gamma = 1.5, method = "rtdr")
identical(auto3, rtdr3)
#> [1] TRUE

# Branch: gamma < 0, 0.1 <= alpha < 1, fewer than 5 draws per setup
#   -->  expects Sun Algorithm 3
set.seed(7); auto4 <- rmhn(4,  alpha = 0.5, beta = 1, gamma = -1)
set.seed(7); sun4  <- rmhn(4,  alpha = 0.5, beta = 1, gamma = -1, method = "sun")
identical(auto4, sun4)
#> [1] TRUE

The four TRUE outputs are the same invariant that the package’s tests enforce as a regression test.

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610926.2021.1934700

Gao, F., & Wang, H.-B. (2025). Generating modified-half-normal random variates by a relaxed transformed density rejection method. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation, 1–25. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610918.2025.2524551

Robert, C. P. (1995). Simulation of truncated normal variables. Statistics and Computing, 5(2), 121–125. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00143942
